Science.title: JWST tracks more than 100 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy
Science.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers identified 104 magnified stellar events in a galaxy known as the Dragon, located around 6.5 billion light-years away. This discovery more than doubles the previous record of 44 such detections in the same galaxy. Because these kinds of events reveal some of the most luminous stars and likely the presence of dark matter, this study offers a rare look at the galaxy's stellar population along with a possible hint at the nature of dark matter.

Science.title: Liquid-assisted crystal growth cuts perovskite defects for efficient solar cells and LEDs

Science.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground

Science.title: 'Stupendously large' primordial black holes ruled out as a dark matter source
Science.summary: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. If they exist, their dramatic origins would set them apart from the black holes we see today, which form when massive stars collapse. Some theories suggest that "stupendously large" primordial black holes could account for a significant share of the universe's elusive dark matter.

Science.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Science.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
Science.summary: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

Science.title: 100 buses long: Scientists map one of the world's largest known coral colonies
Science.summary: A huge coral colony stretching more than 1.5 kilometers (0.93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been identified by researchers, making it one of the largest known coral colonies ever recorded.

Science.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
Science.summary: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.

Science.title: The hidden ways insects support animal life—from habitat to health—go way beyond being food
Science.summary: There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth, and they play highly diverse roles in sustaining the natural world. Insects provide many well-known benefits—what scientists often call "ecosystem services." For example, you can thank a bee or a hoverfly for pollinating wildflowers and agricultural crops, or credit dung beetles for decomposing manure and other waste materials.

Science.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
Science.summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

Science.title: Who is King Ghidorah? The cosmic connections of Godzilla Minus Zero's foe
Science.summary: Godzilla will go toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero. This three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its name.

Science.title: Game theory helps SETI search for alien civilizations
Science.summary: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun-like stars for signs of intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

Science.title: Why the tropics lose the most birds when cities expand
Science.summary: Tropical ecosystems are famous for their teeming, exuberant diversity. In fact, the dramatic increase in biodiversity from the poles to the tropics—known as the latitudinal diversity gradient—is pervasive across branches of the tree of life, and fossil evidence suggests it has existed for millennia.

Science.title: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
Science.summary: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

Science.title: Personalized savings reminders can help boost retirement savings
Science.summary: Private retirement savings are an increasingly important topic in public debate. One popular idea is to phrase savings reminders in one of two ways: either you emphasize what someone stands to lose if they don't save, or you emphasize what they stand to gain if they do. To date, research into which of the two reminder messages is more effective in terms of influencing people's efforts to save has produced conflicting results.

Science.title: Different text genres help doctoral students adapt their writing to reach new readers
Science.summary: An academic abstract, a blog post and a public outreach article all place different demands on the writer. Readers' prior knowledge varies, as does the purpose of the text and what needs explaining. Mastering one kind of text therefore does not automatically mean being able to write another.

Science.title: How frequently did Viking women fight in battle?
Science.summary: The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how frequently did Viking women take part in battles?

Science.title: Would you learn to lucid dream if you could?
Science.summary: Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.
